li.a: National Park Service: War in the Coalfields, the Ludlow Massacre and its impact on the eight-hour workday
Colorado Public Radio: Remembering the Ludlow Massacre 100 years later
Colorado Newsline: 1914 Ludlow Massacre took lives of 25 miners and family members
Library of Congress: Ludlow Massacre, Topics in Chronicling America

content.p: On the morning of 20 April 1914, in a tent colony on the prairie outside Ludlow, Colorado, a day of gunfire began between striking coal miners and the Colorado National Guard. By nightfall the guardsmen had set the camp on fire. In a pit beneath one of the tents lay the bodies of eleven children and two women, according to the Library of Congress. The deaths gave the event its name, and the name was coined, the Colorado Encyclopedia says, by Denver's Rocky Mountain News rather than by the miners.

Nobody agrees on a single death toll, and nobody can say who fired first. What is clear from the sources is that the killings capped a bitter strike against the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company, owned chiefly by John D. Rockefeller Jr., set off ten days of open fighting across southern Colorado, and drew the attention of Congress. The strike itself ended without the union winning what it had asked for.

The National Park Service says Colorado's coal industry employed almost 16,000 people in 1910, close to a tenth of the state's jobs. In 1912 the death rate among the state's coal miners was double the national average. Colorado State Historian William Convery told Colorado Public Radio that more than 1,700 miners died in Colorado mine accidents between the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th, many in explosions of coal dust and methane.

Convery described the working life behind those numbers. Miners often worked 12-hour days, six or seven days a week, and were paid 80 cents for each ton of coal rather than by the hour. The company weighed a ton at 2,200 pounds, not the standard 2,000. Work that made a mine safer, such as laying track, timbering and wetting down dust, was known as "dead work" because it earned nothing.

The Park Service calls Colorado Fuel and Iron one of the most powerful mining companies of the period and one of the worst violators of mine safety rules, with about 70,000 acres under its control. A 1914 report by the US House Committee on Mines and Mining, quoted by Colorado Newsline, said Colorado had good mining laws that ought to protect miners, but that the state's share of fatalities was larger than any other, "showing there is undoubtedly something wrong" in how its mines were run.

In September 1913 the United Mine Workers of America presented demands that included enforcing the eight-hour day, pay for time spent in the shafts, and the right to choose their own housing and doctors. The Park Service reports that the company rejected them all. Britannica dates the walkout to 13 September 1913 and says about 10,000 miners joined it.

Because the company owned the towns, strikers lost their homes. Colorado Newsline says 1,200 miners and their families were evicted and went into tent colonies for the winter of 1913 to 1914. Ludlow was the largest, Britannica says, housing about 1,200 strikers, with a large number of Greeks and Italians. Convery told Colorado Public Radio that the union placed the camps near canyon mouths to watch strikebreakers heading for the mines, that the strikers were well armed, and that the winter was one of the hardest on record.

The company hired and armed 300 members of the Baldwin-Felts detective agency, according to Colorado Newsline. Convery said the private guards beat strikers and drove past the camps at night firing at random to "strike fear into the hearts of the miners". The most notorious vehicle was the Death Special, an armored car with a machine gun. The Colorado Encyclopedia says it shot up the Forbes camp on 17 October 1913, killing one person.

Governor Elias Ammons sent in the National Guard. The Colorado Encyclopedia argues that it did more harm than good: mine owners had arranged to pay for the deployment, and many guardsmen were Spanish-American War and Philippine veterans who saw the multi-ethnic miners as inferiors. Convery said many guardsmen were on the company payroll. Colorado Newsline says the Rockefellers paid the Guard's wages, and that it arrested hundreds of strikers. Britannica adds that in April 1914 the cost of keeping the troops in place led to a smaller Guard presence and more violence.

On Sunday 19 April, Britannica says, guardsmen encircled the camp and set up a machine gun on a bluff above it. The next day was Greek Easter, according to Colorado Newsline. Convery told Colorado Public Radio that the militia came looking for a strikebreaker believed to be hiding in the camp, and that shots were fired. Britannica reports that some accounts say officers demanded the miners hand over at least one person, and the miners refused. The Colorado Encyclopedia puts it plainly: "Nobody knows who fired the first shot."

A daylong battle followed. Militia fired into the colony from high ground while strikers shot back from behind an embankment near the railway, Convery said. Around midday a Colorado and Southern train came through the middle of the fighting. The engineer stopped it, Convery said, which gave strikers cover to retreat east into the hills. Colorado Newsline reports that the train also shielded some family members. Many of the families were left in the crossfire.

The colony's residents had dug cellars under the tents for cover. After the strikers were driven off, Convery said, the guardsmen entered the camp and set fire to the tents. Britannica says they soaked them in kerosene first. The Colorado Encyclopedia says the guardsmen, thinking the colony abandoned, did not know that people were hiding. According to Convery, four women and eleven children were in one pit; all the children and two of the women died. Mary Petrucci, whose three children were among the dead, walked out alive along with one other woman, her granddaughter told Colorado Public Radio. The Colorado Encyclopedia says the victims suffocated from fumes, rather than being shot down "in cold blood" as the miners alleged.

The Colorado Encyclopedia describes the "cold-blooded execution of three leaders under a flag of truce" as the clearest sign of the Guard's hostility, and says Louis Tikas was shot three times in the back. Britannica is more cautious. It says three strike leaders, Tikas among them, were captured and killed by the Guard, and that anecdotal evidence suggests Tikas had been lured out to discuss a truce.
The sources do not agree.

ul.li: The Colorado Encyclopedia counts at least nineteen dead, including one guardsman, five miners and thirteen women and children.
The Park Service says 21, including 11 children.
Britannica and Colorado Newsline say 25, including 11 children; Britannica says three of the dead were guardsmen.

content.p: The totals also change when the fighting afterwards is included. Colorado Newsline cites an estimate of between 69 and 199 deaths for the whole conflict, and Britannica says as many as 50 people died in the response to the massacre. The Colorado Encyclopedia says it is impossible to know how many died in the days after, though certainly more than at Ludlow itself.

News of the fire spread, and the miners hit back. Britannica says they attacked anti-union town officials, strikebreakers and mines, and held an area roughly 50 miles long and 5 miles wide. Convery said they took to the hills and began attacking mine properties systematically. The Colorado Encyclopedia reports that supervisors and guards were shot, property was destroyed, and innocent people died on both sides.

The Colorado Newsline account says the fighting lasted ten days. On 28 April, the Colorado Encyclopedia says, President Wilson sent the US Army. Britannica says the federal troops, unlike the Guard, were impartial and kept strikebreakers out of the mines. The Park Service says Wilson ordered them to disarm both sides.
content.h2: Hearings, trials and the company plan
content.p: Congress held hearings, but Britannica says it took no concrete action. The House Committee on Mines and Mining questioned John D. Rockefeller Jr. for several hours on 20 May 1914, Colorado Newsline reports. He admitted he had not visited the site since the incidents, and, according to a New York Times report quoted there, when asked whether he knew thousands of his employees were living in tents, said he could not say and that company officials could provide the facts. The committee issued a report in 1915, which the Park Service calls instrumental in promoting child labor laws and the eight-hour day. The federal Commission on Industrial Relations also held hearings. The Colorado Encyclopedia says its investigation, led by Frank Walsh, was still keeping the story in the papers years afterwards. Quoted by Colorado Newsline, the commission described the strike as one "against arbitrary power".

The courts offered little accountability. Britannica says the trials of more than 400 miners dragged on until 1920 and none were convicted, while twelve guardsmen were exonerated before a court-martial. Colorado Public Radio, quoting Convery, gives a fuller picture: union organizer John R. Lawson was convicted of murdering a deputy sheriff and sentenced to hard labor, but the Colorado Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 1917; twenty-two guardsmen, ten of them officers, were court-martialed and all but one acquitted; and Lt. Karl Linderfelt was found guilty of assaulting Tikas and received a light reprimand. The union gained about 4,000 members but little else; the Colorado Encyclopedia says the strike ended in December 1914 with none of its stated goals achieved.

Public anger fell on Rockefeller. The Colorado Encyclopedia says the writer Upton Sinclair and others protested outside his New York office and took part in a mock murder trial near his upstate hometown. Rockefeller then hired W. L. Mackenzie King, a former labor minister who later became Canada's prime minister, to design what became known as the Rockefeller Plan, an employee-representation scheme that critics called a company union. The Colorado Encyclopedia says the union ran a nationwide speaking tour by female survivors, and Colorado Public Radio reports that Mother Jones travelled the country telling the story and testified before Congress.

Colorado Newsline says that in 1915 United Mine Workers officers bought 40 acres on the colony's site, and three years later dedicated a granite monument where the women and children died. After the first shock, it says, the strike drew little public attention for decades, until late in the 20th century. The Park Service calls the site a National Historic Landmark, and says the union is now drawing up a master plan for its preservation and interpretation, funded by a 2024 federal planning grant. The Library of Congress now publishes a research guide to the massacre built on digitized 1914 newspapers.
Colorado Newsline links the miners' demands to the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, which gave workers a federal right to bargain over wages, hours and conditions.
